              <f:selectItem itemValue="4" itemLabel="quatre"/>
              <f:selectItem itemValue="5" itemLabel="cinq"/>
            </h:selectManyListbox>
            <p><input type="button" value="#{msg['form.buttonRazText']}" onclick="this.form['formulaire:selectManyListBox'].selectedIndex=-1;" /></p>
          </h:panelGroup>
          <h:outputText value="#{form.selectManyListBoxValue}"/>

    and its template in [Form.java]:

    
private String[] selectManyListBox=new String[]{"1","3"};

    When the [index.xhtml] page is requested for the first time, the resulting page is as follows:

    • Line 2 of the XHTML code generates [1]
    • The text [2] is generated by line 4. The list [3] is generated by lines [5-11]. The attribute size="3" causes the list to display three of these elements at any given time. The elements selected in the list were determined by calling the getSelectManyListBox() method (line 5) of the Java model. The resulting {"1","3"} (line 1 of the Java code) is an array of elements of type String. Each of these elements is used to select one of the items in the list. Here, the items in lines 6 and 10 whose itemValue attribute is in the array {"1","3"} will be selected. This is what [3] shows.
    • Line 14 of the code XHTML generates [4]. Here, the method getSelectManyListBox of the Java model of the list is not called, but rather the following method getSelectManyListBoxValue: 
    
private String[] selectManyListBox=new String[]{"1","3"};
  ...
  // getters and setters
  
  public String getSelectManyListBoxValue(){
    return getValue(selectManyListBox);
  }
  
  private String getValue(String[] chaines){
    String value="[";
    for(String chaine : chaines){
      value+=" "+chaine;
    }
    return value+"]";
  }

    If we had called the getSelectManyListBox method, we would have obtained an array of String. To include this element in the HTML stream, the controller would have called its toString method. However, for an array, this method only returns its "hashcode" and not the list of its elements as we desire. Therefore, we use the getSelectManyListBoxValue method above to obtain a string representing the array’s contents,

    • line 12 of the XHTML code generates the [5] button. When this button is clicked, the Javascript code in the onclick attribute is executed. It will be embedded within the HTML page, which will be generated by the JSF code. To understand this, we need to know the exact nature of that page.

    The HTML feed generated by the XHTML page is as follows:

    
<tr>
<td class="col1"><span class="info">selectManyListBox (size=3)</span></td>
<td class="col2">choix multiple : <select id="formulaire:selectManyListBox" name="formulaire:selectManyListBox" multiple="multiple" size="3">
    <option value="1" selected="selected">un</option>
    <option value="2">deux</option>
    <option value="3" selected="selected">trois</option>
    <option value="4">quatre</option>
    <option value="5">cinq</option>
</select>
            <p><input type="button" value="Raz" onclick="this.form['formulaire:selectManyListBox'].selectedIndex=-1;" /></p>
          </td>
<td class="col3">[ 1 3]</td>
</tr>
    • lines 3 and 9: the HTML <select multiple="multiple"...>...</select> tag generated by the JSF <h:selectManyListBox> tag. It is the presence of the multiple attribute that indicates that this is a multiple-select list,
    • and the fact that the list model is the array String {"1","3"} means that the list items on lines 4 (value="1") and 6 (value="3") have the selected="selected" attribute,
    • line 10: when the [Raz] button is clicked, the code Javascript in the onclick attribute is executed. The page is represented in the browser by an object tree often called DOM (Document Object Model). Each object in the tree is accessible to the code via its attribute. The list on line 3 of the code above is called form:selectManyListBox. The form itself can be referred to in various ways. Here, it is referred to using the notation this.form, where `this` refers to the button [Raz] and this.form refers to the form in which this button is located. The list form:selectManyListBox is located in this same form. Therefore, the notation this.form['formulaire:selectManyListBox'] refers to the location of the list in the form’s component tree. The object representing a list has an attribute selectedIndex whose value is the number of the selected item in the list. This number starts at 0 to denote the first item in the list. The value -1 indicates that no item is selected in the list. The code Javascript, which sets the value -1 for the attribute selectedIndex, deselects all items in the list, if any.

    Now, below, let’s select new values from the list (to select multiple items in the list, hold down the Ctrl key while clicking) and submit the form using the [Valider] [2] button. We receive the following page in response:

    The value of the [1] field submitted is as follows:

    formulaire%3AselectManyListBox=3&formulaire%3AselectManyListBox=4&formulaire%3AselectManyListBox=5

    The validation of the form by [2] caused the [Form.java] model to be updated by the entry [1]. The elements HTML 

    
    <option value="3">trois</option>

    2.5.18. <h:inputHidden> tag

    The <h:inputHidden> tag has no visual representation. It is used solely to insert a <input type="hidden" value="..."/> tag into the page’s HTML flow. When included within a <h:form> tag, their values are part of the data sent to the server when the form is submitted. Because these are form fields that the user cannot see, they are called hidden fields. The purpose of these fields is to preserve data between the different request/response cycles of the same client:

    • the client requests a form F. The server sends it and places information I in a hidden field C, in the form <h:inputHidden id="C" value="I"/>,
    • when the client has filled out form F and submits it to the server, the value I of field C is sent back to the server. The server can then retrieve the information I that it had stored on the page. This creates a memory between the two request/response cycles,
    • JSF uses this technique itself. The information I that it stores in form F is the value of all its components. It uses the following hidden field for this purpose: 
    
<input type="hidden" name="javax.faces.ViewState" id="javax.faces.ViewState" value="H4sIAAAAAAAAANV...8PswawAA" />

    The hidden field is named javax.faces.ViewState, and its value is a string that represents, in encoded form, the value of all the components on the page sent to the client. When the client sends the page back after entering data into the form, the hidden field javax.faces.ViewState is sent back along with the entered values. This is what allows the JSF controller to reconstruct the page as it was originally sent. This mechanism was explained on page 72.

    The code JSF from the example is as follows:

    
<!-- line 9 -->
          <h:outputText value="inputHidden"  styleClass="info"/>
          <h:inputHidden id="inputHidden" value="#{form.inputHidden}"/>
          <h:outputText value="#{form.inputHidden}"/>

    The template for the <h:inputHidden> tag in [Form.java] is as follows:

    
  private String inputHidden="initial";

    This results in the following display when the page [index.xhtml] is first requested:

    • Line 2 generates [1], line 4 generates [2]. Line 3 does not generate any visual elements.

<td class="col2"><input id="formulaire:inputHidden" type="hidden" name="formulaire:inputHidden" value="initial" /></td>
<td class="col3">initial</td>
</tr>

    When the form is submitted, the value "initial" of the field named form:inputHidden on line 3 will be posted along with the other values in the form. The field 

    
  private String inputHidden;

    will be updated with this value, which is the one it already had initially. This value will be included in the new page sent back to the client. We therefore always get the screenshot above.

    The value posted for the hidden field is as follows:

    formulaire%3AinputHidden=initial

    • Line 2 of the code XHTML generates [1],
    • the text [2] is generated by line 4. The checkbox [3] is generated by line [5]. Here, the method getSelectBooleanCheckbox from [Form.java] was used to check or uncheck the checkbox. Since the method returns a boolean value of true (see Java code), the checkbox was checked,
    • line 7 of the XHTML code generates [4]. Once again, the getSelectBooleanCheckbox method from [Form.java] is used to generate the text [4].

    The HTML stream generated by the previous JSF code is as follows:

    
<tr>
<td class="col1"><span class="info">selectBooleanCheckbox</span></td>
<td class="col2"><span class="prompt">mari&eacute;(e) : </span>
<input id="formulaire:selectBooleanCheckbox" type="checkbox" name="formulaire:selectBooleanCheckbox" checked="checked" /></td>
<td class="col3">true</td>

    In [4], we see the tag HTML <input type="checkbox"> that was generated. The value "true" of the associated model caused the attribute checked="checked" to be added to the tag. This causes the checkbox to be checked.

    Now, below, let’s uncheck the [1] checkbox, submit the [2] form, and look at the result obtained [3, 4]:

    Because the checkbox is unchecked, no value is posted for the [1] field.

    Validating the form via [2] caused the [Form.java] template to be updated by the entry [1]. The field selectBooleanCheckbox in [Form.java] was then assigned the value false. The re-display of [index.xhtml] shows that the selectBooleanCheckbox field of the template was indeed updated to [3] and [4]. It is worth noting here that it is thanks to the hidden field javax.faces.ViewState that JSF was able to determine that the initially checked checkbox had been unchecked by the user. Indeed, the value of an unchecked checkbox is not included in the values posted by the browser. Thanks to the component tree stored in the hidden field javax.faces.ViewState, JSF determines that there was a checkbox named "selectBooleanCheckbox" in the form and that its value is not included in the values posted by the client browser. It can conclude that it was unchecked in the posted form, which allows it to assign the Boolean value false to the associated Java model:

    
  private boolean selectBooleanCheckbox;

This tag has a value attribute whose value is a collection of elements of type javax.faces.model.SelectItem. Above, the value of the value attribute is obtained by calling the following [form].getSelectOneListbox1Items method:

    
  public SelectItem[] getSelectOneListbox1Items() {
    return getItems("A",3);
  }
 
  private SelectItem[] getItems(String label, int qte) {
    SelectItem[] items=new SelectItem[qte];
    for(int i=0;i<qte;i++){
      items[i]=new SelectItem(i,label+i);
    }
    return items;
}
    • In line 1, the method getSelectOneListbox1Items returns an array of elements of type javax.faces.model.SelectItem constructed by the private method getItems in line 5. Note that the getSelectOneListbox1Items method is not the getter for a private field selectOneListBox1Items,
    • The class javax.faces.model.SelectItem has various constructors.

    We use line 8 of the getItems method, the constructor SelectItem(Object value, String label), which corresponds to the JSF tag 

    
    <f:selectItem itemValue="value" labelValue="label"/>
    • Lines 5–10: The method getItems(String label, int qte) constructs an array of qte elements of type SelectItem, where element i is obtained by the constructor SelectItem(i, label+i).

  }
  
  public SelectItem[] getSelectManyListBoxItems() {
    return getItems("C",5);
  }
  
  public SelectItem[] getSelectOneMenuItems() {
    return getItems("D",3);
  }
  
  public SelectItem[] getSelectManyMenuItems() {
   return getItems("E",4);
   }
  
  public SelectItem[] getSelectManyCheckboxItems() {
   return getItems("F",3);
   }
  
  public SelectItem[] getSelectOneRadioItems() {
   return getItems("G",4);
   }
  
  private SelectItem[] getItems(String label, int qte) {
    SelectItem[] items=new SelectItem[qte];
    for(int i=0;i<qte;i++){
      items[i]=new SelectItem(i,label+i);
    }
    return items;
}

    Readers are invited to test this new version.

    Most often, the dynamic elements of a form are the results of business logic or come from a database:

    Let’s examine the initial request for the page JSF [index.xhtml] via a GET from the browser:

    • the page JSF is requested [1],
    • the controller [Faces Servlet] requests its display in [3]. The JSF engine that processes the page calls the [Form.java] model of that page, for example the getSelectOneListBox1Items method. This method could very well return an array of elements of type SelectItem, based on information stored in a database. To do this, it would call upon the [métier] and [2b] layers.

    2.7.3.2. Lifetime of the [Form.java] template for the [form*.xhtml] pages

    Consider the following sequence of actions:

    • In [1], fill out page 1 and proceed to page 3,
    • in [2], we fill out page 3 and return to page 1,
    • in [3], page 1 is restored as it was entered. We then return to page 3,
    • in [4], page 3 is found exactly as it was entered.

    The mechanism of the hidden field [javax.faces.ViewState] is not sufficient to explain this phenomenon.

    When switching from [1] to [2], several steps occur:

    • the template [Form.java] is updated with POST from [form1.jsp]. Notably, the field inputText receives the value "another text",
    • the "form3" key in navigation causes [form3.xhtml] to be displayed. The ViewState embedded in [form3.xhtml] reflects the state of only the components of [form3.xhtml], not those of [form1.xhtml].

    When transitioning from [2] to [3]:

    • the [Form.java] model is updated with the POST from [form3.xhtml]. If the [Form.java] template has reached the end of its lifecycle, a brand-new [Form.java] object is created before being updated from [form3.xhtml] to POST. In this case, the inputText field of the template reverts to its default value: 
    
  private String inputText="texte";

    and keeps it: in fact, in POST from [form3.xhtml], nothing updates the inputText field, which is part of the [form1.xhtml] template and not that of [form3.xhtml],

    • the key for navigation, "form1", causes [form1.xhtml] to be displayed. The page displays its template. In our case, the login input field linked to the inputText template will display "text" and not the value "another text" entered in [1]. For the inputText field to retain the value entered in [1], the lifetime of the [Form.java] template must be set to "session" rather than "request." In this case,
      • upon completion of POST from [form1.xhtml], the template will be placed in the client’s session. The field inputText will have the value "another text",
      • when POST runs from [form3.xhtml], the template will be retrieved from this session and updated by POST running from [form3.xhtml]. The inputText field will not be updated by this POST but will retain the value "other text" acquired at the end of POST from [form1.xhtml] [1].

    The declaration of the [Form.java] bean is therefore as follows:

    
package forms;
 
import javax.enterprise.context.SessionScoped;
import javax.faces.bean.ManagedBean;
import javax.faces.model.SelectItem;
 
@ManagedBean
@SessionScoped
public class Form {

    Line 8 gives the bean a session scope.

    2.7.4. Exception Handling

    Let’s revisit the general architecture of a JSF application:

    What happens when an event handler or a model catches an exception originating from the business layer, such as an unexpected disconnection from a database?

    • [2a] event handlers can intercept any exception propagated from the [métier] layer and return a navigation key to the [Faces Servlet] controller, directing it to aspecific to the exception,
    • For templates, this solution is not viable because when they are called ([3,4]), we are in the rendering phase of a specific page (XHTML) and no longer in the selection phase. How can we change pages while we are in the rendering phase of one of them? A simple solution, though not always suitable, is to ignore the exception, which will then propagate up to the servlet container running the application. The container can be configured to display a specific page when an exception reaches it. This solution is always viable, and we will examine it now.

    2.7.4.1. Configuring the Web Application for Exception Handling

    Configuring a web application for exception handling is done in its [web.xml] file:

    
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<web-app version="3.0" xmlns="http://java.sun.com/xml/ns/javaee" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="http://java.sun.com/xml/ns/javaee http://java.sun.com/xml/ns/javaee/web-app_3_0.xsd">
  <context-param>
    <param-name>javax.faces.STATE_SAVING_METHOD</param-name>
    <param-value>client</param-value>
  </context-param>  
  <context-param>
    <param-name>javax.faces.PROJECT_STAGE</param-name>
    <param-value>Development</param-value>
  </context-param>
  <context-param>
    <param-name>javax.faces.FACELETS_SKIP_COMMENTS</param-name>
    <param-value>true</param-value>
  </context-param> 
  <servlet>
    <servlet-name>Faces Servlet</servlet-name>
    <servlet-class>javax.faces.webapp.FacesServlet</servlet-class>
    <load-on-startup>1</load-on-startup>
  </servlet>
  <servlet-mapping>
    <servlet-name>Faces Servlet</servlet-name>
    <url-pattern>/faces/*</url-pattern>
  </servlet-mapping>
  <session-config>
    <session-timeout>
      30
    </session-timeout>
  </session-config>
  <welcome-file-list>
    <welcome-file>faces/form1.xhtml</welcome-file>
  </welcome-file-list>
  <error-page>
    <error-code>500</error-code>
    <location>/faces/exception.xhtml</location>
  </error-page>
  <error-page>
    <exception-type>java.lang.Exception</exception-type>
    <location>/faces/exception.xhtml</location>
  </error-page>
</web-app>

    Lines 32–39 contain the definition of two error pages. You can have as many <error-page> tags as needed. The <location> tag specifies the page to display in case of an error. The error type associated with the page can be defined in two ways:

    • using the <exception-type> tag, which defines the Java type of the handled exception. Thus, the <error-page> tag in lines 36–39 indicates that if the servlet container catches an exception of type [java.lang.Exception] or a derived type (line 37) during application execution, then it must display the page [/faces/exception.xhtml] (line 38). By using the most generic exception type, [java.lang.Exception], here, we ensure that all exceptions are handled,
    • using the <error-code> tag (line 33), which defines an error code HTTP. For example, if a browser requests URL [http://machine:port/contexte/P] and page P does not exist in the application context, the application does not intervene in the response. The servlet container generates this response by sending a default error page. The first line of the response’s HTTP stream contains a 404 error code indicating that the requested page P does not exist. You may want to generate a response that, for example, follows the application’s style guide or provides links to resolve the issue. In this case, use a <error-page> tag with a <error-code>404</error-code> tag.

    Above, the HTTP code for error 500 is the code returned in the event of an application "crash." This is the code that would be returned if an exception were propagated up to the servlet container. The two <error-page> tags on lines 28–35 are therefore likely redundant. We included both to illustrate the two ways to handle an error.

    2.7.4.3. Information related to an exception

    When an exception is propagated to the servlet container, the container displays the corresponding error page by passing information about the exception to it. This information is added as new attributes to the request currently being processed. The browser’s request and the response it will receive are encapsulated in Java objects of type [HttpServletRequest request] and [HttpServletResponse response]. These objects are available at all stages of processing the browser’s request.

    Upon receiving the HTTP request from the browser, the servlet container encapsulates it in the Java object [HttpServletRequest request] and creates the object [HttpServletResponse response], which will be used to generate the response. This object notably contains the channel TCP-IP to be used for the response stream HTTP. All layers t1, t2, ..., tn involved in processing the request object have access to these two objects. Each of them can access the elements of the initial request and prepare the response by enriching the response object. A localization layer, for example, can set the localization of the response using the response.setLocale(Locale l) method.

    The various layers ti can pass information to one another via the request object. This object has an attribute dictionary, which is empty upon creation, that can be populated by successive processing layers. These layers can place information necessary for the next processing layer into the attributes of the request object. There are two methods for managing the attributes of the request object:

    • void setAttribute(String s, Object o), which allows adding an object o identified by the string s to the attributes,
    • Object getAttribute(String s), which retrieves the attribute o identified by the string s.

    When an exception is propagated up to the servlet container, the container sets the following attributes in the request being processed:

    key
    value
    javax.servlet.error.status_code
    the error code HTTP that will be returned to the client
    javax.servlet.error.exception
    the Java type of the exception along with the error message.
    javax.servlet.error.request_uri
    the URL requested when the exception occurred
    javax.servlet.error.servlet_name
    the servlet that was processing the request when the exception occurred

    We will use these request attributes on the [exception.xhtml] page to display them.

    Its content is as follows:

      xmlns:h="http://java.sun.com/jsf/html"
      xmlns:f="http://java.sun.com/jsf/core">
  <f:view locale="#{changeLocale.locale}">
    <h:head>

          <h:outputText value="#{requestScope['javax.servlet.error.status_code']}"/>

    2.7.4.4.1. Expressions on the exception page

    In the client request processing chain, page XHTML is normally the last link in the chain:

    All elements in the chain are Java classes, including the page XHTML. This page is converted into a servlet by the servlet container, c.a.d, into a standard Java class. More specifically, the page XHTML is converted into Java code that runs within the following method:

    
public void _jspService(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
throws java.io.IOException, ServletException {
 
JspFactory _jspxFactory = null;
PageContext pageContext = null;
HTTPSession session = null;
ServletContext application = null;
ServletConfig config = null;
JspWriter out = null;
Object page = this;
JspWriter _jspx_out = null;
PageContext _jspx_page_context = null;
... 
...code de la page XHTML

    Starting on line 14, you will find the Java code for the XHTML page. This code will have a number of objects initialized by the _jspService method, line 1 above:

    • line 1: HttpServletRequest request: the request currently being processed,
    • line 1: HttpServletResponse response: the response that will be sent to the client,
    • line 7: ServletContext application: an object representing the web application itself. Like the request object, the application object can have attributes. These are shared by all requests across all clients instances. They are generally read-only attributes,
    • line 6: HTTPSession session: represents the client’s session. Like the request and application objects, the session object can have attributes. These are shared by all requests from the same client,
    • line 9: JspWriter out: a write stream to the client browser. This object is useful for debugging a XHTML page. Anything written via out.println(text) will be displayed in the client browser.

    When writing #{expression} in the JSF page, expression can be the key of an attribute of the request, session, or application objects mentioned above. The corresponding attribute is searched for successively in these three objects. Thus, #{key} is evaluated as follows:

    1. request.getAttribute(key)
    2. session.getAttribute(key)
    3. application.getAttribute(key)

    As soon as a non-null value is found, the evaluation of #{key} stops. You may want to be more specific by indicating the context in which the attribute should be searched:

    • #{requestScope['clé']} to search for the attribute in the request object,
    • #{sessionScope['clé']} to search for the attribute in the session object,
    • #{applicationScope['clé']} to search for the attribute in the application object.

    This is what was done on page [exception.xhtml], page 116. The attributes used are as follows:

    key
    domain
    value
    javax.servlet.error.status_code
    request
    See section 2.7.4.3.
    javax.servlet.error.exception
    same
    same
    javax.servlet.error.request_uri
    same
    same
    javax.servlet.error.servlet_name
    same
    same

   background-color: #ccffcc
}

   color: #ff0000
}
 
.saisie{
   background-color: #ffcccc;
   border-color: #000000;

    2.8.4. The page [index.xhtml] and its template [Form.java]

    The page [index.xhtml] is as follows:

    The main new feature is the use of tags:

    • to display error messages <h:messages> (line 14), <h:message> (lines 24, 29, 34),
    • which enforce validation constraints on input <f:validateLongRange> (line 39), <f:validateDoubleRange>, <f:validateLength>, <f:validateRegex>,
    • which define a converter between the input and its template as <f:convertDateTime>.

    The template for this page is the following [Form.java] class:

@ManagedBean
@RequestScoped
public class Form {
 
public Form() {
}
// foreclosures
private Integer saisie1 = 0;
private Integer saisie2 = 0;

private Integer saisie4 = 0;

private Double saisie6 = 0.0;
private Boolean saisie7 = true;
private Date saisie8 = new Date();
private String saisie9 = "";
private Integer saisie10 = 0;
private Integer saisie11 = 0;
private Integer saisie12 = 0;
private String errorSaisie11 = "";
private String errorSaisie12 = "";
 
// actions
public String submit() {
...
}
 
public String cancel() {
...
}
 
// validators
public void validateSaisie10(FacesContext context, UIComponent component, Object value) {
...
}
// getters and setters
...
}

    The new feature here is that the model fields are no longer exclusively of type String but of various types.

    2.8.5. The different form entries

    We will now examine the different form inputs one by one.

    2.8.5.1. Entries 1 through 4: entering an integer

    The [index.xhtml] page displays entry 1 in the following format:

    
<!-- line 2 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie1.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie1" value="#{form.saisie1}" styleClass="saisie"/>
        <h:message for="saisie1" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie1}"/>

    The template form.saisie1 is defined as follows in [Form.java]:

    
private Integer saisie1 = 0;

    In a GET browser, the page [index.xhtml] associated with its template [Form.java] visually produces the following:

    • line 2 produces [1],
    • line 3 produces [2],
    • line 4 produces [3],
    • line 5 produces [4].

    Suppose the following entry is made and then validated:

    The result returned in the form by the application is then:

    • [1], the incorrect entry,
    • in [2], the error message indicating it,
    • in [3], we see that the value of the Integer field "entered1" in the model has not changed.

    Let’s explain what happened. To do this, let’s return to the processing cycle of a page JSF:

    We examine this cycle for the component:

    
<h:inputText id="saisie1" value="#{form.saisie1}" styleClass="saisie"/>

    and its model:

    
private Integer saisie1 = 0;
    • In [A], the [index.xhtml] page sent during the browser’s GET is restored. In [A], the page is as the user received it. The component id="saisie1" reverts to its initial value "0",
    • in [B], the page components receive the values posted by the browser. In [B], the page is as the user entered and validated it. The component id="saisie1" receives the posted value "x",
    • in [C], if the page contains explicit validators and converters, these are executed. Implicit converters are also executed if the type of the field associated with the component is not of type String. This is the case here, where the field form.saisie1 is of type Integer. JSF will attempt to convert the value "x" of the component id="saisie1" to an Integer type. This will cause an error that will stop the [A-F] processing cycle. This error will be associated with the id="saisie1" component. Via [D2], we then proceed directly to the response rendering phase. The same page [index.xhtml] is returned;
    • the [D] phase only occurs if all components of a page have passed the conversion/validation phase. It is in this phase that the value of the id="saisie1" component will be assigned to its form.saisie1 template.

    If the [C] phase fails, the page is re-displayed and the following code is executed again:

    
<!-- line 2 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie1.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie1" value="#{form.saisie1}" styleClass="saisie"/>
        <h:message for="saisie1" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie1}"/>

    The message displayed in [2] comes from line 4 of [index.xhtml]. The <h:message for="idComposant"/> tag displays the error message associated with the component specified by the for attribute, if an error occurs. The message displayed in [2] is standard and is located in the [javax/faces/Messages.properties] file within the [jsf-api.jar] archive:

    In [2], we can see that the message file exists in several variants. Let’s examine the contents of [Messages_fr.properties]:

    The file contains messages divided into categories:

    • errors on a component, line 3,
    • conversion errors between a component and its model, line 12
    • validation errors when validators are present on the page, line 23.

    The error that occurred on the id="saisie1" component is a conversion error from a String type to an Integer type. The associated error message is the one on line 18 of the message file.

    javax.faces.converter.IntegerConverter.INTEGER_detail={2} : «{0}» doit être un nombre compris entre -2147483648 et 2147483647. Exemple : {1}

    The error message that was displayed is reproduced below:

    We can see in the message:

    • the {2} parameter has been replaced by the ID of the component for which the conversion error occurred,
    • the parameter {0} has been replaced by the entry made in [1] for the component,
    • the parameter {1} has been replaced by the number 9346.

    Most component-related messages have two versions: a summary version (version) and a detailed version (version). This is the case for lines 16–18:

    1
2
    javax.faces.converter.IntegerConverter.INTEGER={2} : «{0}» doit être un nombre composé d’un ou de plusieurs chiffres.
javax.faces.converter.IntegerConverter.INTEGER_detail={2} : «{0}» doit être un nombre compris entre -2147483648 et 2147483647. Exemple : {1}

    The message with the key _detail (line 2) is the so-called detailed message. The other is the so-called summary message. The <h:message> tag displays the detailed message by default. This behavior can be changed using the showSummary and showDetail attributes. This is what is done for the id input2 component:

    
        <!-- line 3 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie2.prompt']}" />
        <h:inputText id="saisie2" value="#{form.saisie2}"  styleClass="saisie"/>
        <h:message for="saisie2" showSummary="true" showDetail="false" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie2}"/>

    Line 2: The saisie2 component is linked to the following field: form.saisie2

    
  private Integer saisie2 = 0;

    The result obtained is as follows:

    • in [1], the detailed message; in [2], the summary message.

    The <h:messages> tag displays all summarized error messages from all components, as well as error messages not linked to a component, in the form of a list. Here again, attributes can change this default behavior:

    • showDetail: true / false to enable or disable detailed messages,
    • showSummary: true / false to request or not request summarized messages,
    • globalOnly: true / false to specify whether to display only error messages not associated with components. Such a message could, for example, be created by the developer.

    The error message associated with a conversion can be changed in various ways. First, you can instruct the application to use a different message file. This change is made in [faces-config.xml]:

    
<faces-config ...">
  <application>
    <resource-bundle>
      <base-name>
        messages
      </base-name>
      <var>msg</var>
    </resource-bundle>
    <message-bundle>messages</message-bundle>
  </application>
...
</faces-config>

    Lines 3–8 define a message file, but this is not the one used by the <h:message> and <h:messages> tags. You must use the <message-bundle> tag on line 9 to define it. Line 9 tells the <h:message(s)> tags that the file [messages.properties] must be parsed before the file [javax.faces.Messages.properties]. So if we add the following lines to the file [messages_fr.properties]:

    
# conversions
javax.faces.converter.IntegerConverter.INTEGER=erreur
javax.faces.converter.IntegerConverter.INTEGER_detail=erreur d\u00e9taill\u00e9e

    the error returned for the input1 and input2 components becomes:

    Another way to modify the conversion error message is to use the component’s converterMessage attribute as shown below for the input3 component:

    
        <!-- line 4 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie3.prompt']}" />
        <h:inputText id="saisie3" value="#{form.saisie3}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}"/>
        <h:message for="saisie3" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie3}"/>

    The saisie3 component is linked to the following form.saisie3 field:

    
  private Integer saisie3 = 0;
    • line 3, the converterMessage attribute explicitly sets the message to display in the event of a conversion error,
    • line 3, the required="true" attribute indicates that the field is required. The field cannot be left empty. A field is considered empty if it contains no characters or if it contains a sequence of spaces. Here again, there is a default message in [javax.faces.Messages.properties]: 
    javax.faces.component.UIInput.REQUIRED={0} : erreur de validation. Vous devez indiquer une valeur.

    The requiredMessage attribute allows you to replace this default message. If the [messages.properties] file contains the following messages:

    
...
data.required=Vous devez entrer une donnée
integer.required=Vous devez entrer un nombre entier

    we can get the following result:

    or this one:

    Verifying that an entry is indeed an integer is not always sufficient. Sometimes it is necessary to verify that the entered number falls within a given range. In such cases, a validator is used. Entry #4 provides an example. Its code in [index.xhtml] is as follows:

    
        <!-- line 5 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie4.prompt']}" />
        <h:inputText id="saisie4" value="#{form.saisie4}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}" validatorMessage="#{msg['saisie4.error']}">
          <f:validateLongRange minimum="1" maximum="10" />
        </h:inputText>
        <h:message for="saisie4" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie4}"/>

    Line 3, the saisie4 component is linked to the following form.saisie4 model:

    
  private Integer saisie4 = 0;

    Lines 3–5: The <h:inputText> tag has a child tag, <f:validateLongRange>, which accepts two optional attributes: minimum and maximum. This tag, also known as a validator, allows you to apply a constraint to the input value: it must not only be an integer, but an integer within the range [minimum, maximum] if both the minimum and maximum attributes are present; greater than or equal to minimum if only the minimum attribute is present; and less than or equal to maximum if only the maximum attribute is present. The <f:validateLongRange> validator has default error messages in [javax.faces.Messages.properties]:

    1
2
3
    javax.faces.validator.LongRangeValidator.MINIMUM={1} : erreur de validation. La valeur est inférieure à la valeur minimale autorisée, "{0}".
javax.faces.validator.LongRangeValidator.NOT_IN_RANGE={2} : erreur de validation. L’attribut spécifié n’est pas compris entre les valeurs attendues {0} et {1}.
javax.faces.validator.LongRangeValidator.TYPE={0} : erreur de validation. La valeur n’est pas du type correct.

    Again, it is possible to replace these messages with others. There is an attribute, validatorMessage, that allows you to define a specific message for the component. Thus, with the following code:

    
        <h:inputText id="saisie4" value="#{form.saisie4}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}" validatorMessage="#{msg['saisie4.error']}">
          <f:validateLongRange minimum="1" maximum="10" />
</h:inputText>

    and the following message in [messages.properties]:

    saisie4.error=4-Vous devez entrer un nombre entier dans l'interval [1,10]

    the following result is obtained:

    2.8.5.2. Inputs 5 and 6: Entering a real number

    The entry of real numbers follows rules similar to those for entering integers. The code XHTML for entries 5 and 6 is as follows:

    
<!-- line 6 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie5.prompt']}" />
        <h:inputText id="saisie5" value="#{form.saisie5}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['double.required']}"/>
        <h:message for="saisie5" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie5}"/>
        <!-- line 7 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie6.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie6" value="#{form.saisie6}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['double.required']}" validatorMessage="#{msg['saisie6.error']}">
          <f:validateDoubleRange minimum="0.0"/>
        </h:inputText>
        <h:message for="saisie6" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie6}"/>

    Elements of the [Form.java] model related to the saisie5 and saisie6 components:

    
  private Double saisie5 = 0.0;
  private Double saisie6 = 0.0;

    Error messages associated with the converters and validators for the saisie5 and saisie6 components in [messages.properties]:

    
double.required=Vous devez entrer un nombre
saisie6.error=6-Vous devez entrer un nombre >=0

    Here is an example of execution:

    2.8.5.3. Input 7: Entering a Boolean

    A Boolean should normally be entered using a checkbox. If entered using an input field, the string "true" is converted to the Boolean value true, and any other string is converted to the Boolean value false.

    The XHTML code from the example:

    
<!-- line 8 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie7.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie7" value="#{form.saisie7}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['double.required']}"/>
        <h:message for="saisie7" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie7}"/>

    The saisie7 component template:

    
  private Boolean saisie7 = true;

    Here is an example of an input and its response:

    In [1], the entered value. Upon conversion, this "x" string becomes the Boolean false. This is shown by [2]. The value [3] of the model has not changed. It only changes when all conversions and validations on the page have succeeded. This was not the case in this example.

    2.8.5.4. Entry 8: Entering a date

    In the example, a date is entered using the following code: XHTML:

    
<!-- line 9 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie8.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie8" value="#{form.saisie8}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['date.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['saisie8.error']}">
          <f:convertDateTime pattern="dd/MM/yyyy"/>
        </h:inputText>
        <h:message for="saisie8" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie8}">
          <f:convertDateTime pattern="dd/MM/yyyy"/>
        </h:outputText>

    The saisie8 component on line 3 uses a java.lang.String <--> java.util.Date converter. The form.saisie8 template associated with the saisie8 component is as follows:

    
  private Date saisie8 = new Date();

    The component defined by lines 7–9 also uses a converter, but only in the direction java.util.Date --> java.lang.String.

    The <f:convertDateTime> converter supports various attributes, including the pattern attribute, which specifies the format of the string to be converted into a date or the format in which a date should be displayed.

    When the [index.xhtml] page is first requested, the previous line 8 is displayed as follows:

    The fields [1] and [2] both display the value of the form.saisie8 template:

    
  private Date saisie8 = new Date();

    where entry8 takes the value of the current date. The converter used in both cases to display the date is as follows:

    
            <f:convertDateTime pattern="dd/MM/yyyy"/>

    where dd (day) denotes the day number, MM (Month) the month number, and yyyy (year) the year. In [1], the converter is used for the reverse conversion from java.lang.String --> java.util.Date. The entered date must therefore follow the format "dd/MM/yyyy" to be valid.

    There are default messages for invalid dates in [javax.faces.Messages.properties]:

    1
2
    javax.faces.converter.DateTimeConverter.DATE={2} : «{0}» n’a pas pu être interprété en tant que date.
javax.faces.converter.DateTimeConverter.DATE_detail={2} : «{0}» n’a pas pu être interprété en tant que date. Exemple : {1}

    which can be replaced with your own messages. For example:

    
<h:inputText id="saisie8" value="#{form.saisie8}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['date.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['saisie8.error']}">
  <f:convertDateTime pattern="dd/MM/yyyy"/>
</h:inputText>

    the message displayed in the event of a conversion error will be the message with the key saisie8.error, as follows:

    
saisie8.error=8-Vous devez entrer une date valide au format jj/mm/aaaa

    Here is an example:

    2.8.5.5. Input 9: Entering a string with a restricted length

    Entry 9 shows how to enforce a character count within a specified range for an entered string:

    
<!-- line 10 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie9.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie9" value="#{form.saisie9}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" validatorMessage="#{msg['saisie9.error']}">
          <f:validateLength minimum="4" maximum="4"/>
        </h:inputText>
        <h:message for="saisie9" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie9}"/>

    Line 4: The validator <f:validateLength minimum="4" maximum="4"/> requires the entered string to have exactly 4 characters. You can use only one of the attributes: minimum for a minimum number of characters, maximum for a maximum number.

    The form.saisie9 template for the saisie9 component on line 3 is as follows:

    
  private String saisie9 = "";

    There are default error messages for this type of validation:

    1
2
    javax.faces.validator.LengthValidator.MAXIMUM={1} : erreur de validation. La longueur est supérieure à la valeur maximale autorisée, "{0}".
javax.faces.validator.LengthValidator.MINIMUM={1} : erreur de validation. La longueur est inférieure à la valeur minimale autorisée, "{0}".

    which can be replaced using the validatorMessage attribute as shown in line 3 above. The message for the key saisie9.error is as follows:

    
saisie9.error=9-Vous devez entrer une chaîne de 4 caractères exactement

    Here is an example of execution:

    2.8.5.6. Input 9B: Entering a string that must conform to a pattern

    Input 9B shows how to require that an entered string have a number of characters within a range:

    
<!-- line 10B -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie9B.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie9B" value="#{form.saisie9B}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" validatorMessage="#{msg['saisie9B.error']}">
          <f:validateRegex pattern="^\s*\d{2}:\d{2}\s*$"/>
        </h:inputText>
        <h:message for="saisie9B" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie9B}"/>

    Line 4: The validator <f:validateRegex pattern="^\s*\d{2}:\d{2}\s*$"/> requires the entered string to match a regular expression pattern, in this case: a sequence of 0 or more spaces, 2 digits, the colon (:), 2 digits, a sequence of 0 or more spaces.

    The pattern form.saisie9B for the saisie9B component in line 3 is as follows:

    
private String saisie9B;

javax.faces.validator.RegexValidator.PATTERN_NOT_SET_detail=La valeur définie du modèle d’expression régulière ne peut pas être vide.

    which can be replaced using the attribute validatorMessage as in line 3 above. The message for key saisie9.error is as follows:

    2.8.5.7. Entry 10: Write a specific validation method

    To summarize: JSF allows you to verify, among the entered values, the validity of numbers (integers, real numbers), dates, string lengths, and the compliance of an entry with a regular expression. JSF allows you to add your own validators and converters to the existing ones. This topic is not covered here, but you can read [ref2] for further details.

    Here we present another method: one that validates entered data using a method from the form model. Here is an example:

    
<!-- line 11 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie10.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie10" value="#{form.saisie10}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" validator="#{form.validateSaisie10}"/>
        <h:message for="saisie10" styleClass="error"/>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie10}"/>

    The form.saisie10 template associated with the saisie10 component in line 3 is as follows:

    
  private Integer saisie10 = 0;

    We want the entered number to be <1 or >7. We cannot verify this using the basic validators of JSF. We therefore write our own validation method for the saisie10 component. We specify this using the validator attribute of the component to be validated:

    
          <h:inputText id="saisie10" value="#{form.saisie10}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" validator="#{form.validateSaisie10}"/>

    The saisie10 component is validated by the form.validateSaisie10 method. This method is as follows:

    
  public void validateSaisie10(FacesContext context, UIComponent component, Object value) {
    int saisie = (Integer) value;
    if (!(saisie < 1 || saisie > 7)) {
      FacesMessage message = Messages.getMessage(null, "saisie10.incorrecte", null);
      message.setSeverity(FacesMessage.SEVERITY_ERROR);
      throw new ValidatorException(message);
    }
}

    The signature of a validation method must be that of line 1:

    • FacesContext context: page execution context—provides access to various information, including the HttpServletRequest request and HttpServletResponse response objects,
    • UIComponent component: the component to be validated. The <h:inputText> tag is represented by a UIInput-type component derived from UIComponent. Here, it is this UIInput component that is received as the second parameter,
    • Object value: the entered value to be validated, converted to the model’s type. It is important to understand here that if the conversion from String to the model’s type fails, then the validation method is not executed. When the validateSaisie10 method is called, it means that the conversion from String to Integer was successful. The third parameter is then of type Integer.
    • Line 2: The entered value is converted to type int,
    • Line 3: Check that the entered value is less than 1 or greater than 7. If so, validation is complete. If not, the validator must report the error by throwing a ValidatorException exception.

    The ValidatorException class has two constructors:

    • the [1] constructor takes an error message of type FacesMessage as a parameter. This message type is the one displayed by the <h:messages> and <h:message> tags,
    • the [2] constructor also allows you to encapsulate the cause of the error, which is of type Throwable or a subclass thereof.

    We need to construct a message of type FacesMessage. This class has several constructors:

    The [1] constructor defines the properties of a FacesMessage object:

    • FacesMessage.Severity severity: a severity level taken from the following enumeration: SEVERITY_ERROR, SEVERITY_FATAL, SEVERITY_INFO, SEVERITY_WARN,
    • String summary: the summarized version of the error message—is displayed by the tags <h:message showSummary="true"> and <h:messages>,
    • String detail: the detailed version of the error message (version) is displayed using the <h:message> and <h:messages showDetail="true"> tags.

    Any of the constructors can be used; missing parameters can be set later using set methods.

    The [1] constructor does not allow you to specify a message that would be in an internationalized message file. This is obviously a shame. David Geary and Cay Horstmann address this shortcoming in their book "Core JavaServer Faces" with the utility class com.corejsf.util.Messages. This is the class used in line 4 of the Java code to create the error message. It contains only static methods, including the getMessage method used in line 4:

    
   public static FacesMessage getMessage(String bundleName, String resourceId, Object[] params)

    The getMessage method accepts three parameters:

    • String bundleName: the name of a message file without its .properties suffix but with its package name. Here, our first parameter could be messages to refer to the file [messages.properties]. Before using the file specified by the first parameter, getMessage attempts to use the application’s message file, if one exists. Thus, if in [faces-config.xml] a message file has been declared with the tag: 
    
  <application>
...
    <message-bundle>messages</message-bundle>
</application>

    you can pass null as the first parameter to the getMessage method. This is what was done here (see [web.xm], page 120),

    • String resourceId: the key of the message to be processed in the message file. We have seen that a message can have both a summarized version and a detailed version. resourceId is the identifier for the summarized version. The detailed version will be automatically retrieved using the key resourceId_detail. Thus, we will have two messages in [messages.properties] for the error on entry #10: 
    
saisie10.incorrecte=10-Saisie n° 10 incorrecte
saisie10.incorrecte_detail=10-Vous devez entrer un nombre entier <1 ou >7

    The message of type FacesMessage generated by the method Messages.getMessage includes both the summary and detailed versions if they were found. Both versions must be present; otherwise, an exception of type [NullPointerException] is thrown,

    • Object[] params: the actual parameters of the message if it has formal parameters {0}, {1}, ... These formal parameters will be replaced by the elements of the params array.

    Let’s return to the code for the validation method of the saisie10 component:

    
  public void validateSaisie10(FacesContext context, UIComponent component, Object value) {
    int saisie = (Integer) value;
    if (!(saisie < 1 || saisie > 7)) {
      FacesMessage message = Messages.getMessage(null, "saisie10.incorrecte", null);
      message.setSeverity(FacesMessage.SEVERITY_ERROR);
      throw new ValidatorException(message);
    }
}
    • In [4], the message of type FacesMessage is created using the static method Messages.getMessage,
    • in [5], the message severity level is set,
    • in [6], an exception of type ValidatorException is thrown with the message constructed previously. The validation method was called by the following XHTML code: 
    
<!-- line 11 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie10.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie10" value="#{form.saisie10}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" validator="#{form.validateSaisie10}"/>
        <h:message for="saisie10" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie10}"/>

    Line 3: The validation method is executed for the id input10 component. Therefore, the error message generated by the validateSaisie10 method is associated with this component and is thus displayed by line 4 (for="saisie10" attribute). The detailed version is displayed by default by the <h:message> tag.

    Here is an example of execution:

    2.8.5.8. Entries 11 and 12: Validating a Group of Components

    So far, the validation methods we’ve encountered have only validated a single component. What if the desired validation involves multiple components? That’s what we’ll look at now. In the form:

    we want entries 11 and 12 to be two integers whose sum equals 10.

    The code JSF will be as follows:

    
<!-- line 12 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie11.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie11" value="#{form.saisie11}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}"/>
        <h:panelGroup>
          <h:message for="saisie11" styleClass="error"/>
          <h:outputText value="#{form.errorSaisie11}" styleClass="error"/>
        </h:panelGroup>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie11}"/>
        <!-- line 13 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie12.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie12" value="#{form.saisie12}" styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}"/>
        <h:panelGroup>
          <h:message for="saisie12" styleClass="error"/>
          <h:outputText value="#{form.errorSaisie12}" styleClass="error"/>
        </h:panelGroup>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie12}"/>

    and the associated model:

    
  private Integer saisie11 = 0;
  private Integer saisie12 = 0;
  private String errorSaisie11 = "";
private String errorSaisie12 = "";

    In line 3 of the JSF code, we use the techniques already presented to verify that the value entered for the input11 component is indeed an integer. The same applies, on line 11, to the input12 component. To verify that input11 + input12 = 10, we could build a specific validator. This is the preferred solution. Again, we will refer to [ref2] to discover it. Here, we are taking a different approach.

    The page [index.xhtml] is validated by a button [Valider], whose code JSF is as follows:

    
<!-- control buttons -->
      <h:panelGrid columns="2">
        <h:commandButton value="#{msg['submit']}" action="#{form.submit}"/>
        ...
      </h:panelGrid>

    where the message msg['submit'] is as follows:

    
submit=Valider

    As seen in line 3, the method form.submit will be executed to handle the click on the [Valider] button. It is as follows:

    
  // actions
  public String submit() {
    // latest validations
    validateForm();
    // we return the same form
    return null;
  }
 
  // global validations
  private void validateForm() {
    if ((saisie11 + saisie12) != 10) {
...
}

    It is important to understand that when the submit method runs:

    • all form validators and converters have been executed and passed,
    • the fields in the [Form.java] template have received the values posted by the client.

    In fact, let’s return to the processing cycle of a POST JSF:

    The submit method is an event handler. It handles the click event on the [Valider] button. Like all event handlers, it runs in the [E] phase, once all validators and converters have been executed and succeeded ([C]) and the model has been updated with the posted values ([D]). Therefore, we no longer need to throw exceptions of type [ValidatorException] as we did previously. We will simply return the form with error messages:

    In [1], we will alert the user, and in [2] and [3], we will set an error flag. In the code JSF, the message [1] will be obtained as follows:

    
<h:form id="formulaire">
      <h:messages globalOnly="true" />
      <h:panelGrid columns="4" columnClasses="col1,col2,col3,col4" border="1">
        <!-- line 1 -->
        ...

    On line 2, the <h:messages> tag displays by default the version summary of error messages for all incorrect entries in form components as well as all error messages not related to components. The attribute globalOnly="true" limits the display to the latter.

    The messages [2] and [3] are displayed with simple <h:outputText> tags:

    
<!-- line 12 -->
        <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie11.prompt']}"/>
        <h:inputText id="saisie11" value="#{form.saisie11}"  styleClass="saisie" required="true" requiredMessage="#{msg['data.required']}" converterMessage="#{msg['integer.required']}"/>
        <h:panelGroup>
          <h:message for="saisie11" styleClass="error"/>
          <h:outputText value="#{form.errorSaisie11}" styleClass="error"/>
        </h:panelGroup>
        <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie11}"/>
        <!-- line 13 -->
        ...
          <h:outputText value="#{form.errorSaisie12}" styleClass="error"/>
        ...

    Lines 4–7: The input11 component has two possible error messages:

    • one indicating an incorrect conversion or missing data. This message, generated by JSF itself, will be contained in a FacesMessage type and displayed by the <h:message> tag on line 5,
    • the one we will generate if entry11 + entry12 does not equal 10. It will be displayed by line 6. The error message will be contained in the form.errorSaisie11 template.

    The two messages correspond to errors that cannot occur at the same time. The check for input11 + input12 = 10 is performed in the submit method, which runs only if there are no remaining errors in the form. When it runs, the entry11 component will have been checked and its template form.saise11 will have received its value. The message on line 5 will no longer be displayed. Conversely, if the message on line 5 is displayed, then at least one error remains in the form and the submit method will not run. The message on line 6 will not be displayed. To ensure that the two possible error messages are in the same column of the table, they have been grouped within an <h:panelGroup> tag (lines 4 and 7).

    The submit method is as follows:

    
  // actions
  public String submit() {
    // latest validations
    validateForm();
    // we return the same form
    return null;
  }
 
  // global validations
  private void validateForm() {
    if ((saisie11 + saisie12) != 10) {
      // global msg
      FacesMessage message = Messages.getMessage(null, "saisies11et12.incorrectes", null);
      message.setSeverity(FacesMessage.SEVERITY_ERROR);
      FacesContext context = FacesContext.getCurrentInstance();
      context.addMessage(null, message);
      // field-related msg
      message = Messages.getMessage(null, "error.sign", null);
      setErrorSaisie11(message.getSummary());
      setErrorSaisie12(message.getSummary());
    } else {
      setErrorSaisie11("");
      setErrorSaisie12("");
    }
}
    • line 4: the method submit calls the method validateForm to perform the final validations,
    • line 11: checks if input11 + input12 = 10,
    • if not, lines 13–14, a message of type FacesMessage is created with the message from id saisies11et12.incorrectes. This is as follows: 
    saisies11et12.incorrectes=La propriété saisie11+saisie12=10 n'is not verified
    • The message thus constructed is added (lines 15–16) to the application’s list of error messages. This message is not linked to a specific component. It is a global application message. It will be displayed by the <h:messages globalOnly="true"/> tag shown above,
    • line 18: a new message of type FacesMessage is created with the message id error.sign. This is as follows: 
    
error.sign="!"

    We noted that the static method [Messages.getMessage] constructs a message of type FacesMessage with a summarized version and a detailed version if they exist. Here, only the summarized version of the message error.sign exists. We obtain the summarized version of a message m via m.getSummary(). Lines 19 and 20: the summary version of the message error.sign is placed in the errorSaisie11 and errorSaisie12 fields of the template. They will be displayed by the following JSF tags:

    
          <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie11}"/>
          ...
          <h:outputText value="#{form.saisie12}"/>
    • lines 22-23: if the condition `entry11 + entry12 = 10` is true, then the two fields `errorSaisie11` and `errorSaisie12` in the template are cleared so that any previous error message is removed. It is important to note here that the form is retained between requests in the client’s session.

    Here is an example of execution:

    Note in the [1] column that the form has received the posted values, indicating that all validation and conversion operations between the posted values and the form were successful. The event handler form.submit, which handles the click on the [Valider] button, was thus able to execute. It is this event handler that generated the messages displayed in [2] and [3]. We can see that the model was updated even though the form was rejected and sent back to the client. One might want the template not to be updated in such a case. Indeed, assuming the user cancels the update using the [Annuler] or [4] button, it will not be possible to return to the initial template unless it has been saved.

    2.8.5.9. POST for a form without input validation

    Consider the form above and suppose that the user, not realizing their errors, wants to abandon the form entry. They will then use the [Annuler] button generated by the following JSF code:

    
<!-- control buttons -->
      <h:panelGrid columns="2">
        <h:commandButton value="#{msg['submit']}" action="#{form.submit}"/>
        <h:commandButton value="#{msg['cancel']}" immediate="true" action="#{form.cancel}"/>
      </h:panelGrid>

    Line 4, the message msg['cancel'] is as follows:

    
cancel=Annuler

    The method form.cancel associated with the button [Annuler] will only be executed if the form is valid. This is what we demonstrated for the form.submit method associated with the [Valider] button. If the user wants to cancel the form submission, there is of course no need to check the validity of their entries. This result is achieved using the immediate="true" attribute, which instructs JSF to execute the form.cancel method without going through the validation and conversion phase. Let’s return to the processing cycle of POST JSF:

    The events of the action components <h:commandButton> and <h:commandLink> with the attribute immediate="true" are processed in the [C] phase, then the JSF cycle proceeds directly to the [E] response rendering phase.

    The form.cancel method is as follows:

    
  public String cancel() {
    saisie1 = 0;
    saisie2 = 0;
    saisie3 = 0;
    saisie4 = 0;
    saisie5 = 0.0;
    saisie6 = 0.0;
    saisie7 = true;
    saisie8 = new Date();
    saisie9 = "";
    saisie10 = 0;
    return null;
}

    If you use the [Annuler] button in the previous form, you get the following page in return:

    • the form is displayed again because the event handler form.cancel sets the key of navigation to null. The page [index.xhtml] is therefore returned,
    • the template [Form.java] was modified by the method form.cancel. This is reflected in the column [2], which displays this template,
    • while the [3] column reflects the posted value for the components.

    Let’s go back to the code JSF for the input1 component [4];

    
          <!-- line 1 -->
          <h:outputText value="#{msg['saisie1.prompt']}"/>
          <h:inputText id="saisie1" value="#{form.saisie1}" styleClass="saisie"/>
          <h:message for="saisie1" styleClass="error"/>
<h:outputText value="#{form.saisie1}"/>

    Line 4: The value of the saisie1 component is linked to the form.saisie1 template. This results in several things:

    • during a GET from [index.xhtml], the input1 component will display the value of the form.saisie1 template,
    • during a POST from [index.xhtml], the posted value for the input1 component is assigned to the form.saisie1 template only if all form validations and conversions succeed. Regardless of whether the template has been updated by the posted values, if the form is returned at the end of POST, the components display the value that was posted and not the value of the template associated with them. This is shown in the screenshot above, where the [2] and [3] columns do not have the same values.

    2.9. Example mv-jsf2-07: events related to the state change of JSF components

    2.9.1. The application

    The application shows an example of POST implemented without using a button or a link. The form is as follows:

When the selection in [1] is changed, a POST of the form is executed, during which the content of combo2 is modified to reflect the item selected in [1], and then the form is returned. During this POST, no validation is performed.

    The new feature is in the code for combo1, lines 24–26. New attributes appear:

    • onchange: attribute HTML - declares a function or code Javascript that must be executed when the selected item in combo1 changes. Here, the code Javascript submit() submits the form to the server,
    • valueChangeListener: JSF attribute - declares the name of the method to be executed on the server side when the selected item in combo1 changes. In total, two methods are executed: one on the client side, the other on the server side,
    • immediate=true: attribute JSF - sets the timing for when the server-side event handler should be executed: after the form has been reconstructed as the user entered it but before the input validation checks. The goal here is to populate the combo2 list based on the item selected in the combo1 list, even if there are invalid entries elsewhere in the form. Here is an example:
    • in [1], an initial entry,
    • in [2], we change the selected item in combo1 from A to B.

    The result is as follows:

    POST has been executed. The content of combo2 ([2]) was adjusted to match the selected item in combo1 ([1]), even though the entry ([3]) was incorrect. It was the immediate=true attribute that caused the form.combo1ChangeListener method to be executed before the validity checks. Without this attribute, it would not have been executed because the processing cycle would have stopped at the validity checks due to the error in [3].

    2.9.5. The [Form.java] template

    The [Form.java] template is as follows:

    
package forms;
 
import java.util.logging.Logger;
import javax.enterprise.context.RequestScoped;
import javax.faces.bean.ManagedBean;
import javax.faces.context.FacesContext;
import javax.faces.event.ValueChangeEvent;
import javax.faces.model.SelectItem;
 
@ManagedBean
@RequestScoped
public class Form {
  
  public Form() {
  }
  
// form fields
  private String combo1="A";
  private String combo2="A1";
  private Integer saisie1=0;
  
  // working fields
  final private String[] combo1Labels={"A","B","C"};
  private String combo1Label="A";
  private static final Logger logger=Logger.getLogger("forms.Form");
  
  // methods
  public SelectItem[] getCombo1Items(){
    // init combo1
    SelectItem[] combo1Items=new SelectItem[combo1Labels.length];
    for(int i=0;i<combo1Labels.length;i++){
      combo1Items[i]=new SelectItem(combo1Labels[i],combo1Labels[i]);
    }
    return combo1Items;
  }
  
  public SelectItem[] getCombo2Items(){
    // init combo2 as a function of combo1
    SelectItem[] combo2Items=new SelectItem[5];
    for(int i=1;i<=combo2Items.length;i++){
      combo2Items[i-1]=new SelectItem(combo1Label+i,combo1Label+i);
    }
    return combo2Items;
  }
  
  // listeners
  public void combo1ChangeListener(ValueChangeEvent event){
    // follow-up
    logger.info("combo1ChangeListener");
    // retrieve the posted value of combo1
    combo1Label=(String)event.getNewValue();
    // we return the answer because we want to short-circuit the validations
    FacesContext.getCurrentInstance().renderResponse();
  }
  
  public String raz(){
    // follow-up
    logger.info("raz");
    // raz du formulaire
    combo1Label="A";
    combo1="A";
    combo2="A1";
    saisie1=0;
    return null;
  }
  
// getters - setters
  ...
}

    Let's link the [index.xhtml] form to its [Form.java] template:

    The combo1 list is generated by the following JSF code:

    
        <h:selectOneMenu id="combo1" value="#{form.combo1}" immediate="true" onchange="submit();" valueChangeListener="#{form.combo1ChangeListener}" styleClass="combo">
          <f:selectItems value="#{form.combo1Items}"/>
</h:selectOneMenu>

    It obtains its elements via the getCombo1Items method of its model (line 2). This method is defined in lines 28–35 of the Java code. It generates a list of three elements {"A", "B", "C"}.

    The combo2 list is generated by the following JSF code:

    
        <h:selectOneMenu id="combo2" value="#{form.combo2}" styleClass="combo">
          <f:selectItems value="#{form.combo2Items}"/>
</h:selectOneMenu>

    It obtains its items via the getCombo2Items method of its model (line 2). This method is defined in lines 37–44 of the Java code. It generates a list of five items {"X1", "X2", "X3",X4","X5"} where X is the combo1Label element from line 16. Therefore, when the form is initially generated, the combo2 list contains the elements {"A1","A2","A3","A4","A5"}.

    When the user changes the selected item in the combo1 list,

    • the onchange="submit();" event will be handled by the client browser. The form will then be submitted to the server,
    • and on the server side, JSF will detect that the combo1 component has changed its value. The combo1ChangeListener method in lines 47–54 will be executed. A method of type ValueChangeListener receives an object of type javax.faces.event.ValueChangeEvent as a parameter. This object allows you to retrieve the old and new values of the component that has changed using the following methods:

    Here, the component is the combo1 list of type UISelectOne. Its value is of type String.

    • Line 51 of the Java template: the new value of combo1 is stored in combo1Label, which is used to generate the elements of the combo2 list,
    • line 53: the response is returned. It is important to note here that the combo1ChangeListener handler is executed with the attribute immediate="true". It is therefore executed after the phase in which the page component tree has been updated with the posted values and before the validation process for the posted values. However, we want to bypass this validation process because the combo2 list must be updated even if there are still invalid entries elsewhere in the form. We therefore request that the response be sent immediately without going through the data validation phase.
    • The form will be sent back exactly as it was entered. However, the elements in combo1 and combo2 are not posted values. They will be regenerated by calling the methods getCombo1Items and getCombo2Items. The latter method will then use the new value from combo1Label set by combo1ChangeListener, and the items in the combo2 list will change.

    2.9.6. The [Raz] button

    We want to use the [Raz] button to reset the form to its initial state, as shown below:

    In [1], the form before the POST of the [Raz] button; in [2], the result of POST.

    Although functionally simple, handling this use case proves to be quite complex. We can try various solutions, including the one used for the [Annuler] button in the previous example:

    
       <h:commandButton value="#{msg['raz']}" immediate="true" action="#{form.raz}"/>

    where the form.raz method is as follows:

    
  public String raz(){
    // raz du formulaire
    combo1Label="A";
    combo1="A";
    combo2="A1";
    saisie1=0;
    return null;
}

    The result obtained by the [Raz] button in the previous example is as follows:

    The [1] column shows that the form.raz method was executed. However, the [1] column continues to display the posted values:

    • for combo1, the posted value was "B". This element is therefore selected in the list,
    • for combo2, the posted value was "B5". Due to the execution of form.raz, the elements {"B1", ..., "B5"} of combo2 were changed to {"A1", ..., "A5"}. The element "B5" no longer exists and therefore cannot be selected. The first element in the list is then displayed,
    • for entry1, the posted value was 10.

    This is the normal behavior with the immediate="true" attribute. To get a different result, you must submit the values you want to see in the new form even if the user has entered different values. This is achieved with a little Javascript client-side code. The form becomes the following:

    
<script language="javascript">
  function raz(){
    document.forms['formulaire'].elements['formulaire:combo1'].value="A";
    document.forms['formulaire'].elements['formulaire:combo2'].value="A1";
    document.forms['formulaire'].elements['formulaire:saisie1'].value=0;
    //document.forms['formulaire'].submit();
  }
</script>
...
<h:commandButton value="#{msg['raz']}" onclick='raz()' immediate="true" action="#{form.raz}"/>
    • line 10, the onclick='raz()' attribute instructs the system to execute the Javascript raz function when the user clicks the [Raz] button,
    • Line 3: The value "A" is assigned to the HTML element named 'form:combo1'. The various elements on line 3 are as follows:
      • document: page displayed by the browser,
      • document.forms: set of forms in the document,
      • document.forms['formulaire']: the form with the attribute name="form",
      • documents.forms['formulaire'].elements: set of form elements with the attribute name="form",
      • document.forms['formulaire'].elements['formulaire:combo1']: form element with the attribute name="form:combo1"
      • document.forms['formulaire'].elements['formulaire:combo1'].value: value that will be submitted by the form element with the attribute name="form:combo1".

    To find out the name attributes of the various elements on the page displayed by the browser, you can view its source code (shown below with IE7):

    <form id="formulaire" name="formulaire" ...>
...
<select id="formulaire:combo1" name="formulaire:combo1" ...>

    With this explained, we can see that in the Javascript code of the raz function:

    • line 3 ensures that the value posted for the combo1 component will be the string A,
    • line 4 ensures that the value posted for the combo2 component will be the string A1,
    • line 5 ensures that the value posted for the saisie1 component will be the string 0.

    Once this is done, the form’s POST, associated with any button of type <h:commandButton> (line 10), will be triggered. The form.raz method will be executed, and the form will be returned as it was posted. The following result is then obtained:

    This result hides a lot of information. The values "A", "A1", and "0" from the combo1, combo2, and saisie1 components are posted to the server. Suppose the previous value of combo1 was "B". In that case, there is a change in the value of the combo1 component, and the form.combo1ChangeListener method should also be executed. We have two event handlers with the attribute immediate="true". Will both of them be executed? If so, in what order? Only one? If so, which one?

    To find out more, we create logs in the application:

    
package forms;
 
import java.util.logging.Logger;
...
public class Form {
  
...  
// form fields
  private String combo1="A";
  private String combo2="A1";
  private Integer saisie1=0;
  
  // working fields
  final private String[] combo1Labels={"A","B","C"};
  private String combo1Label="A";
  private static final Logger logger=Logger.getLogger("forms.Form");
  
  // listener
  public void combo1ChangeListener(ValueChangeEvent event){
    // follow-up
    logger.info("combo1ChangeListener");
    // retrieve the posted value of combo1
    combo1Label=(String)event.getNewValue();
    // we return the answer because we want to short-circuit the validations
    FacesContext.getCurrentInstance().renderResponse();
  }
  
  public String raz(){
    // follow-up
    logger.info("raz");
    // raz du formulaire
    combo1Label="A";
    combo1="A";
    combo2="A1";
    saisie1=0;
    return null;
  }
...
}
    • line 16: a log generator is created. The parameter of getLogger allows us to differentiate the origins of the logs. Here, the logger is called forms.Form,
    • line 21: the entry into the method combo1ChangeListener is logged,
    • Line 30: The entry into the raz method is logged.

    What logs are generated by the [Raz] button or by changing the value of combo1? Let’s consider various cases:

    • We use the [Raz] button while the selected item in combo1 is "A". "A" is therefore the last value of the combo1 component. We have seen that the [Raz] button executes a Javascript function that posts the value "A" for the combo1 component. The combo1 component therefore does not change its value. The logs then show that only the form.raz method is executed:
      
    • We use the [Raz] button even though the selected item in combo1 is not "A". The combo1 component therefore changes its value: its last value was not "A", and the [Raz] button will set it to "A". The logs then show that two methods are executed. In order: combo1ChangeListener, reset:
      
    • we change the value of combo1 without using the [Raz] button. The logs show that only the combo1ChangeListener method is executed:

    Now, let’s examine the [Retirer] links column:

    This column is generated by the following code:

...

          </h:commandLink>
